% Section 5: Constraint Composition (§5 in main.tex)
% Draft — OntoCoDec Framework

At each decoding step $t$, both layers produce a binary token mask over the vocabulary $V$.
Let $G(t) \subseteq V$ denote the set of tokens permitted by the grammar layer (valid JSON structure and ontology-vocabulary membership),
and $S(t) \subseteq V$ the set permitted by the semantic layer (domain/range type compliance given the current entity registry state).
The final mask is their conjunction:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:composition}
  M_{\text{final}}(t) = M_{\text{grammar}}(t) \;\wedge\; M_{\text{semantic}}(t),
\end{equation}
%
so that a token is allowed only if it satisfies \emph{both} structural and type-level constraints.
The conjunction is asymmetric in an important sense: the semantic layer operates \emph{strictly within} the grammar-valid set, i.e., $S(t)$ is defined only over $G(t)$.
This reflects the enabling dependency described in \S\ref{sec:overview}: grammar validity is a precondition for semantic enforcement, because the semantic layer must identify the current relation type to look up its domain/range rules—an operation that is only well-defined when the relation type belongs to the ontology vocabulary.

\paragraph{Grammar-First Fallback.}

The conjunction in Eq.~\eqref{eq:composition} requires the precondition $S(t) \cap G(t) \neq \emptyset$: at least one token must be simultaneously grammar-valid and semantically valid.
When this precondition is violated—which can occur under tight ontology constraints where the allowed entity types for a relation do not overlap with the grammar-valid tokens at a particular position—na\"{\i}ve application of the semantic mask sets all grammar-valid tokens to $-\infty$ while grammar-invalid tokens retain finite (though heavily penalized) logits.
The resulting argmax selects a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.
We enforce a \emph{grammar-first fallback rule}: before applying the semantic mask, we verify that at least one semantically allowed type token has a logit above a grammar-validity threshold $\tau_g = -10^{8}$.
If $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$, semantic masking is skipped entirely, and the grammar layer alone controls token selection.
This reflects a deliberate priority ordering: structural integrity (grammar) is a hard constraint, while a type violation is a soft error detectable by downstream validation.


\paragraph{Constraint Tightness.}

We quantify the restrictiveness of semantic constraints with a per-relation \emph{tightness} measure.
For a relation $r \in \mathcal{R}$, let $\mathcal{V}(r)$ denote the set of entity type pairs $(\tau^h, \tau^t)$ observed in the training ontology for relation $r$, and let $\mathcal{T}$ denote the full entity type vocabulary.
We define the tightness of $r$ as:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tightness}
  \tau(r) = 1 - \frac{|\mathcal{V}(r)|}{|\mathcal{T}|^2},
\end{equation}
%
where $\mathcal{V}(r) \subseteq \operatorname{dom}(r) \times \operatorname{range}(r)$ and $\tau(r) \in [0, 1]$: $\tau = 1$ indicates that $r$ admits no valid type pair (a degenerate case), while $\tau = 0$ means all type combinations are permitted and the semantic mask imposes no additional restriction beyond grammar.
Observed pairs are typically a strict subset of $\operatorname{dom}(r) \times \operatorname{range}(r)$: for example, SciERC's \textsc{Used-for} relation has $|\operatorname{dom}| = |\operatorname{range}| = 6$ entity types, yielding a Cartesian product of 36, but only 35 pairs are attested in the data (\emph{Metric}$\times$\emph{Metric} is unobserved).
The mean tightness $\bar{\tau} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|}\sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}} \tau(r)$ characterizes the overall restrictiveness of an ontology's type constraints.
Intuitively, tighter constraints cause the semantic mask $S(t)$ to eliminate a larger fraction of grammar-valid tokens at type-bearing positions, increasing the probability that $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$ and triggering the grammar-first fallback.
Consequently, ontologies with high mean tightness retain higher residual domain/range violation rates despite full constraint enforcement.
Section~\ref{sec:docred-results} demonstrates this empirically: DocRED ($\bar{\tau} = 0.842$, 5.68 valid pairs per relation) achieves 45--90\% DR reduction across models, whereas SciERC ($\bar{\tau} = 0.333$, 24 valid pairs per relation) achieves 94--99\%, with the residual modulated by model-specific baseline violation rates (Section~\ref{sec:cross-model}).


\paragraph{Decidability Taxonomy.}

Not all ontology constraints can be enforced at the same point during autoregressive generation.
We classify them by \emph{when} sufficient information becomes available:
%
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
  \item \textbf{Local constraints} require only the current token. Entity-type and relation-vocabulary membership fall in this class: each candidate token can be checked against the ontology vocabulary independently, which the grammar layer handles via CFG and enum rules.
  \item \textbf{Prefix-decidable constraints} require the current token plus previously generated context. Domain/range constraints are prefix-decidable: once the head entity type and relation type have been generated, the valid tail entity types are fully determined. The semantic layer implements this via a stateful entity registry that tracks decoded types and activates the appropriate logit mask at each type-bearing position.
  \item \textbf{Non-local constraints} require information not yet generated. Forward coreference—where a later mention determines the type of an earlier one—is inherently non-local and falls outside the scope of single-pass left-to-right decoding.
\end{enumerate}
%
OntoCoDec's two-layer design covers the first two classes: grammar for local, semantic for prefix-decidable. The non-local class motivates the two-pass strategy (S2, \S\ref{sec:s2}), which partially addresses cross-field consistency by separating entity extraction from relation generation, though it does not fully resolve forward coreference (\S\ref{sec:limitations}).

% Section 7 — Conclusion
% Data source: Phase 2 SciERC registry experiments + Phase 0 DocRED
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_full_s1,
%          phase0_scierc_unconstrained, phase0_docred_unconstrained
% All numbers verified against registry 2026-05-14.

We presented OntoCoDec, a framework that automatically compiles IE ontology schemas into token-level decoding constraints to enforce type validity at generation time.
Our work makes three contributions.

First, we conducted the first systematic study of ontological constraint violations in LLM-based IE (\S\ref{sec:violation_landscape}).
Across two benchmarks with substantially different ontology sizes---SciERC (7~relations) and DocRED (96~relations)---we found that domain/range violation rates are comparable (15.37\% vs.\ 18.46\%), % exp_ids: phase0_scierc_unconstrained, phase0_docred_unconstrained
indicating that violation severity is driven by \emph{constraint tightness} $\bar{\tau}$ rather than ontology scale.
SciERC ($\bar{\tau}{=}0.333$, mean 24 valid type pairs per relation) and DocRED ($\bar{\tau}{=}0.842$, mean 5.68) exhibit comparable violation rates despite a 14$\times$ difference in ontology size, and within each model, DR reduction scales inversely with $\bar{\tau}$: 94--99\% on SciERC ($\bar{\tau}{=}0.333$) vs.\ 45--90\% on DocRED ($\bar{\tau}{=}0.842$), with the residual modulated by model-specific baseline violation rates (Section~\ref{sec:cross-model}).
% Qwen: SciERC DR↓94%, DocRED DR↓45%; Llama: SciERC DR↓99%, DocRED DR↓90%

Second, we introduced a two-layer constraint architecture that decomposes ontological enforcement into complementary mechanisms:
a \emph{grammar layer} (XGrammar CFG) that eliminates structural violations (RV, ET\,$\to$\,0\%) and a \emph{semantic layer} (TypeConstraintProcessor with a stateful entity registry) that enforces domain/range constraints at the token level. % exp_id: phase2_scierc_grammar_only
The grammar layer serves as an enabling prerequisite for the semantic layer; the two compose via bitwise AND over candidate token sets.

Third, we validated OntoCoDec empirically.
On SciERC, the full system reduces domain/range violations from 15.37\% to 0.93\%---a 94\% relative reduction---while completely eliminating RV and ET violations, with no significant impact on relation F1 ($+$0.13 percentage points, $p > 0.05$). % exp_id: phase2_scierc_full_s1
On DocRED, the full system reduces domain/range violations from 18.46\% to 10.21\%---a 45\% relative reduction---while eliminating RV and ET violations entirely, with statistically significant gains in relation F1 ($+$0.50pp, $p{<}0.001$) and entity F1 ($+$1.23pp, $p{<}0.001$) for Qwen3-8B. Llama-3.1-8B achieves substantial DR reduction (90.2\%, 26.07\%\,$\to$\,2.55\%) with F1-neutral impact. % exp_ids: phase2_docred_full, llama_docred_full_s1, llama_docred_unconstrained
Compared with post-hoc filtering, decoding-time enforcement preserves true positives and eliminates entity-type violations that post-hoc methods cannot address.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
Several limitations qualify these findings.
The semantic layer introduces cross-field consistency (CF) violations: CF rises from 0.08\% under unconstrained decoding to 9.90\% with full constraints. % exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_full_s1
This is a systematic consequence of per-relation independent type enforcement---when the same entity appears across multiple triples, each relation's domain/range constraint may assign it a different type, producing entity-versus-relation type drift.
The grammar layer alone does not elevate CF (0.08\%, matching the unconstrained baseline), confirming that CF is entirely attributable to the semantic layer. % exp_id: phase2_scierc_grammar_only
Resolving this cross-relation type coherence problem is an open challenge, not a trivial implementation fix.
Cross-field consistency violations increase with constraint strength and vary across models: CF reaches 12.02\% for Llama-3.1-8B on DocRED under full constraints, compared with 2.57\% for Qwen3-8B on the same dataset, suggesting that per-relation independent enforcement interacts with model-specific generation patterns. % exp_ids: llama_docred_full_s1, phase2_docred_full
Constrained decoding can increase parse failure rates for some model-dataset combinations: Llama-3.1-8B on DocRED shows 91 parse failures under full constraints versus 68 unconstrained (9.1\% vs.\ 6.8\%), likely due to max-token truncation of longer constrained outputs. All F1 metrics are computed over successfully parsed documents only. % exp_ids: llama_docred_full_s1, llama_docred_unconstrained
Beyond CF, experiments use two models (Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), confirming that constraint enforcement generalizes across model families: Llama-3.1-8B on DocRED achieves a 90.2\% DR reduction (26.07\%\,$\to$\,2.55\%) without any code modification.
% llama_docred_unconstrained: DR=26.07%; llama_docred_full_s1: DR=2.55%
Results are reported for two models and two datasets under zero-shot prompting only, and integration with fine-tuned models has not been explored.

\paragraph{Future Work.}
We identify four directions.
(1)~Extension to larger models (quantized 70B-class) to further verify model-agnostic generalization across scales.
(2)~Global entity-level type consensus during decoding---maintaining a shared entity registry across all relations within an instance---to resolve CF violations.
(3)~Integration with fine-tuned models, combining constraint-aware training objectives with decoding-time enforcement.
(4)~Extension to non-English ontologies to evaluate cross-lingual applicability.

% Discussion paragraphs for §7
% Three standalone paragraphs: (1) Low F1 practical significance,
% (2) CF severity argument, (3) F1 significance difference explanation.
% All quantitative claims traced to registry exp_ids.

%%% Paragraph 1: Low F1 Practical Significance %%%
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1 (R-F1=8.36%), phase2_docred_full_s1 (R-F1=8.23%),
%          phase0_scierc_unconstrained (DR=15.37%), phase2_docred_unconstrained (DR=18.46%)

\paragraph{Practical Significance of Zero-Shot F1.}
Our reported relation F1 of approximately 8\% on both SciERC and DocRED reflects the inherent difficulty of zero-shot closed IE, where the model receives no task-specific training examples.
For reference, supervised state-of-the-art systems on SciERC achieve approximately 49--53\% relation F1 with full training data~\citep{zhong2021frustratingly,ye2022packed}.
Constraint enforcement operates largely independently of the extraction model's intrinsic capability: it restricts the output space to ontologically valid triples regardless of the underlying model's accuracy.
When applied to fine-tuned models that reach competitive F1 levels, the same constraints remain necessary---Phase~0 analysis confirms that even well-prompted models exhibit non-trivial violation rates (15.37\% DR on SciERC, 18.46\% on DocRED).
% exp_ids: phase0_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_docred_unconstrained
In our evaluation, F1 serves as a \emph{control variable} verifying that constraint enforcement does not degrade extraction quality, not as an optimization target.
The contribution of this work is the constraint enforcement method itself; the zero-shot setting isolates its effect from confounds introduced by task-specific fine-tuning.

%%% Paragraph 2: CF Severity Argument %%%
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1 (CF=9.90%), phase2_scierc_grammar_only (CF=0.08%),
%          phase2_docred_full_s1 (CF=2.57%)

\paragraph{Severity of Cross-Field Violations.}
Domain/range (DR) violations produce structurally invalid triples---a triple asserting that a \emph{Task} entity fills the \emph{domain} slot of \textsc{Part-of}, which requires \emph{Method}, cannot be consumed by any downstream system without error.
DR violations are therefore hard constraints.
Cross-field consistency (CF) violations are qualitatively different: each individual triple remains type-valid with respect to its own relation's domain/range rules; only cross-triple consistency is broken when the same entity receives different types across relations.
The dominant conflict pattern---\emph{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$\emph{OtherScientificTerm} (60 of 245~affected entities on SciERC)---reflects genuine semantic ambiguity in the type system rather than a systematic method failure.
% exp_id: phase2_scierc_full_s1
Ablation evidence cleanly attributes CF to the semantic layer: grammar-only decoding yields CF\,=\,0.08\%, matching the unconstrained baseline, while the full system reaches 9.90\% on SciERC and 2.57\% on DocRED
(Qwen3-8B; Llama-3.1-8B exhibits 12.02\% on DocRED, the highest across all configurations).
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_grammar_only, phase2_docred_full_s1
% llama_docred_full_s1: CF=0.1202
This arises from per-relation independent enforcement, where each relation's constraint mask is computed without access to type decisions made for other relations.
A natural extension is a global entity-level type consensus pass that resolves entity types before relation-specific enforcement.

%%% Paragraph 3: F1 Significance Difference Explanation %%%
% exp_ids: d012_bootstrap_ci (DocRED +0.50pp p<0.001, SciERC +0.13pp p=0.58),
%          phase0_docred_unconstrained (RV=29.66%), phase0_scierc_unconstrained (RV=1.39%)

\paragraph{Dataset-Dependent F1 Impact.}
The divergence in F1 significance between DocRED ($+$0.50\,pp, $p < 0.001$, 95\% CI [$+$0.23, $+$0.81]) and SciERC ($+$0.13\,pp, $p = 0.58$, 95\% CI [$-$0.24, $+$0.58]) traces to a single mechanism: grammar-layer elimination of out-of-vocabulary (OOV) relation names.
% exp_id: d012_bootstrap_ci
Under the all-valid-set evaluation protocol, a predicted triple whose relation name does not appear in the ontology is counted as a false positive.
The DocRED baseline exhibits a relation-vocabulary (RV) violation rate of 29.66\%---5{,}189 predictions with OOV relation names---all of which become false positives under this protocol.
% exp_id: phase0_docred_unconstrained
The grammar layer eliminates these OOV predictions, removing a substantial source of false positives and yielding a statistically significant precision gain.
On SciERC, the baseline RV rate is only 1.39\% (24~OOV predictions), too few to produce a detectable F1 effect.
% exp_id: phase0_scierc_unconstrained
The F1 improvement on DocRED is thus a direct, mechanistically transparent consequence of vocabulary enforcement at scale, not an artifact of constraint-induced distribution shift.
Llama-3.1-8B's lower baseline RV (16.03\% vs.\ Qwen's 29.66\%)
results in fewer OOV predictions eliminated by the grammar layer,
yielding a smaller but directionally consistent R-F1 improvement
($+$0.29\,pp vs.\ $+$0.50\,pp), confirming that the magnitude of
F1 gain is proportional to the baseline OOV rate.
% llama_docred_unconstrained: RV=0.1603, R-F1=5.98
% llama_docred_full_s1: RV=0, R-F1=6.27, delta=+0.29pp
% qwen_docred: RV=0.2966, R-F1 delta=+0.50pp

%%% Paragraph 4: Decoding-Time vs. Post-Hoc Enforcement %%%
% exp_ids: posthoc_filtering_baseline, phase2_scierc_full_s1 (R-F1=8.36%),
%          phase2_docred_full_s1 (R-F1=8.23%, ET=0%)

\paragraph{Decoding-Time vs.\ Post-Hoc Enforcement.}
Post-hoc filtering---generating triples without constraints, then removing schema-violating predictions---yields higher precision and consequently higher F1 than OntoCoDec on both datasets (SciERC 8.63 vs.\ 8.36; DocRED 9.61 vs.\ 8.23).
% posthoc: SciERC F1=8.63, DocRED F1=9.61; OntoCoDec: SciERC R-F1=8.36, DocRED R-F1=8.23
However, this precision gain comes at substantial cost.
On DocRED, post-hoc filtering discards 48.1\% of all predicted triples, including 127 true positives (11.2\% of correct predictions), reducing recall from 9.46\% to 8.40\%.
% posthoc_docred: rejection=48.1%, tp_lost=127/1137, R: 9.46→8.40
Entity type violations remain unresolved (ET\,=\,2.47\% vs.\ OntoCoDec's 0\%), as filtering targets only domain/range and vocabulary violations.
% posthoc_docred: ET_residual=2.47%; phase2_docred_full_s1: ET=0%
OntoCoDec's decoding-time approach avoids this information loss by guiding generation toward compliant outputs rather than discarding non-compliant ones, preserving both recall and entity type validity.
The two strategies are complementary: post-hoc filtering can serve as an additional safety net for residual violations that decoding-time enforcement does not fully resolve.

\section{Violation Landscape}
\label{sec:violation_landscape}

Before presenting our constrained decoding framework, we first quantify how frequently LLMs violate ontological constraints during information extraction.
This analysis serves two purposes: it establishes the practical severity of unconstrained generation and identifies which constraint categories demand enforcement at decoding time versus those addressable through prompting alone.

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:violation_setup}

We evaluate a strong open-weight model, Qwen3-8B~\cite{qwen2025qwen3}, under zero-shot greedy decoding on two IE benchmarks that differ substantially in ontological complexity:
\textbf{SciERC}~\cite{luan2018scierc} (551 test sentences, 7 relation types, avg.\ 26.1 valid type pairs per relation) and \textbf{DocRED}~\cite{yao2019docred} (998 dev documents, 96 relation types, avg.\ 5.68 valid type pairs per relation).
Both datasets ship with typed entity and relation schemas, enabling automatic constraint checking.

We measure four categories of ontological violation:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Domain/Range (DR):} a predicted triple $(h,r,t)$ satisfies $(\mathrm{type}(h), \mathrm{type}(t)) \notin \sigma(r)$, where $\sigma(r)$ is the set of valid subject--object type pairs for relation $r$.
    \item \textbf{Relation Vocabulary (RV):} the predicted relation type $r \notin \mathcal{R}$.
    \item \textbf{Entity Type (ET):} the predicted entity type $e \notin \mathcal{E}$.
    \item \textbf{Cross-Field Consistency (CF):} the same entity span is assigned different types across distinct triples within one instance.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Violation Distribution}
\label{sec:violation_distribution}

Table~\ref{tab:prompt_comparison} reports violation rates on both benchmarks.
On SciERC (1{,}724 predicted triples, 2{,}474 entities), domain/range violations affect 15.37\% of triples, while RV, ET, and CF violations are comparatively rare at 1.39\%, 0.40\%, and 0.08\%, respectively.
On DocRED (16{,}540 triples, 19{,}099 entities), DR violations reach 18.70\%---comparable to SciERC despite DocRED's ontology being 14$\times$ larger.
This parity suggests that DR violation rates are driven primarily by \emph{constraint tightness} (valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology size: DocRED averages only 5.68 valid pairs per relation versus SciERC's 26.1.

RV violations on DocRED are dramatically higher (28.90\% vs.\ 1.39\%), indicating that 96 relation types exceed the model's capacity to faithfully reproduce a target vocabulary from a single in-context specification.
ET violations follow a similar trend (7.50\% vs.\ 0.40\%).
CF violations remain negligible on both datasets (0.08\%), suggesting that within-instance type coherence is largely maintained even without explicit enforcement.

\subsection{Per-Relation Analysis}
\label{sec:per_relation}

Figure~\ref{fig:per_relation_dr} breaks down DR violation rates by relation type on SciERC.
Violation rates vary by over 40 percentage points across relations:
\textsc{Compare} exhibits the highest rate at 42.4\% (28/66 triples), followed by \textsc{Feature-of} at 33.5\% (163/486), \textsc{Part-of} at 25.0\% (18/72), and \textsc{Evaluate-for} at 24.1\% (32/133).
At the other extreme, \textsc{Used-for} violates at only 0.76\% (6/787) and \textsc{Conjunction} at 0\% (0/32).

This distribution correlates with constraint tightness: \textsc{Compare} permits only a few valid type pairs in the SciERC schema, leaving minimal room for type substitution, whereas \textsc{Used-for} and \textsc{Conjunction} accept a broad range of subject--object type combinations.
The pattern implies that violations are not random generation noise but systematic failures to satisfy narrow type constraints---precisely the setting where decoding-time enforcement is most needed.

\subsection{Prompt Insufficiency}
\label{sec:prompt_insufficiency}

A natural question is whether explicitly stating domain/range constraints in the prompt suffices to eliminate violations.
We test \emph{schema-informed prompting}, which augments the extraction prompt with the full list of valid type pairs for each relation.

On SciERC, schema-informed prompting reduces DR violations from 15.37\% to 5.78\% (a 62.4\% relative reduction) and lowers RV from 1.39\% to 0.30\% and ET from 0.40\% to 0\% (Table~\ref{tab:prompt_comparison}).
On DocRED, the reduction is weaker: DR drops from 18.70\% to 12.84\% ($-$31.3\%), RV from 28.90\% to 18.40\%, and ET from 7.50\% to 0.61\%.
McNemar's test confirms that all four violation-category improvements are statistically significant ($p < 0.01$) on both datasets.

However, aggregate improvements mask per-relation instability.
On SciERC, schema-informed prompting reduces DR for \textsc{Feature-of} by 22.3 percentage points and \textsc{Part-of} by 22.5~pp, but \emph{increases} DR for \textsc{Evaluate-for} by 5.8~pp (Figure~\ref{fig:per_relation_dr}).
This reversal---where adding constraint information to the prompt worsens compliance on a specific relation---demonstrates that prompt-based approaches lack the guarantee of monotonic improvement across all constraint categories.

Two findings emerge from this analysis.
First, prompt-based schema enforcement scales poorly with ontological complexity: the relative DR reduction on DocRED (31.3\%) is roughly half that on SciERC (62.4\%), and RV violations remain at 18.40\% even after prompting.
Second, even on the simpler SciERC ontology, prompt interventions are unreliable at the per-relation level.
These limitations motivate a decoding-time mechanism that enforces constraints \emph{by construction} rather than by instruction, which we present in Section~\ref{sec:method}.

\subsection{Decoding Strategies}
\label{sec:strategies}

We consider two decoding strategies that differ in how entity and relation generation are orchestrated.

\paragraph{S1: Single-pass decoding.}
Both constraint layers are active throughout a single generation pass.
The entity registry is populated as entities are generated and is immediately available for relation-level type checking within the same pass.
This is the simpler and recommended strategy.

\paragraph{S2: Two-pass decoding.}
In the first pass, the model generates only the entity list under grammar-only constraints.
The extracted entities are then used to compile an input-dependent grammar that additionally constrains head and tail entity names to match declared entities.
In the second pass, the model generates relations under this tighter grammar plus semantic constraints.
The two-pass separation aims to provide a more complete entity registry before relation generation begins, potentially improving type consistency.

% Section 5: Constraint Composition (§5 in main.tex)
% Draft — OntoCoDec Framework

At each decoding step $t$, both layers produce a binary token mask over the vocabulary $V$.
Let $G(t) \subseteq V$ denote the set of tokens permitted by the grammar layer (valid JSON structure and ontology-vocabulary membership),
and $S(t) \subseteq V$ the set permitted by the semantic layer (domain/range type compliance given the current entity registry state).
The final mask is their conjunction:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:composition}
  M_{\text{final}}(t) = M_{\text{grammar}}(t) \;\wedge\; M_{\text{semantic}}(t),
\end{equation}
%
so that a token is allowed only if it satisfies \emph{both} structural and type-level constraints.
The conjunction is asymmetric in an important sense: the semantic layer operates \emph{strictly within} the grammar-valid set, i.e., $S(t)$ is defined only over $G(t)$.
This reflects the enabling dependency described in \S\ref{sec:overview}: grammar validity is a precondition for semantic enforcement, because the semantic layer must identify the current relation type to look up its domain/range rules—an operation that is only well-defined when the relation type belongs to the ontology vocabulary.

\paragraph{Grammar-First Fallback.}

The conjunction in Eq.~\eqref{eq:composition} requires the precondition $S(t) \cap G(t) \neq \emptyset$: at least one token must be simultaneously grammar-valid and semantically valid.
When this precondition is violated—which can occur under tight ontology constraints where the allowed entity types for a relation do not overlap with the grammar-valid tokens at a particular position—na\"{\i}ve application of the semantic mask sets all grammar-valid tokens to $-\infty$ while grammar-invalid tokens retain finite (though heavily penalized) logits.
The resulting argmax selects a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.
We enforce a \emph{grammar-first fallback rule}: before applying the semantic mask, we verify that at least one semantically allowed type token has a logit above a grammar-validity threshold $\tau_g = -10^{8}$.
If $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$, semantic masking is skipped entirely, and the grammar layer alone controls token selection.
This reflects a deliberate priority ordering: structural integrity (grammar) is a hard constraint, while a type violation is a soft error detectable by downstream validation.


\paragraph{Constraint Tightness.}

We quantify the restrictiveness of semantic constraints with a per-relation \emph{tightness} measure.
For a relation $r \in \mathcal{R}$, let $\mathcal{V}(r)$ denote the set of entity type pairs $(\tau^h, \tau^t)$ observed in the training ontology for relation $r$, and let $\mathcal{T}$ denote the full entity type vocabulary.
We define the tightness of $r$ as:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tightness}
  \tau(r) = 1 - \frac{|\mathcal{V}(r)|}{|\mathcal{T}|^2},
\end{equation}
%
where $\mathcal{V}(r) \subseteq \operatorname{dom}(r) \times \operatorname{range}(r)$ and $\tau(r) \in [0, 1]$: $\tau = 1$ indicates that $r$ admits no valid type pair (a degenerate case), while $\tau = 0$ means all type combinations are permitted and the semantic mask imposes no additional restriction beyond grammar.
Observed pairs are typically a strict subset of $\operatorname{dom}(r) \times \operatorname{range}(r)$: for example, SciERC's \textsc{Used-for} relation has $|\operatorname{dom}| = |\operatorname{range}| = 6$ entity types, yielding a Cartesian product of 36, but only 35 pairs are attested in the data (\emph{Metric}$\times$\emph{Metric} is unobserved).
The mean tightness $\bar{\tau} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|}\sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}} \tau(r)$ characterizes the overall restrictiveness of an ontology's type constraints.
Intuitively, tighter constraints cause the semantic mask $S(t)$ to eliminate a larger fraction of grammar-valid tokens at type-bearing positions, increasing the probability that $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$ and triggering the grammar-first fallback.
Consequently, ontologies with high mean tightness retain higher residual domain/range violation rates despite full constraint enforcement.
Section~\ref{sec:docred-results} demonstrates this empirically: DocRED ($\bar{\tau} = 0.842$, 5.68 valid pairs per relation) achieves 45--90\% DR reduction across models, whereas SciERC ($\bar{\tau} = 0.333$, 24 valid pairs per relation) achieves 94--99\%, with the residual modulated by model-specific baseline violation rates (Section~\ref{sec:cross-model}).


\paragraph{Decidability Taxonomy.}

Not all ontology constraints can be enforced at the same point during autoregressive generation.
We classify them by \emph{when} sufficient information becomes available:
%
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
  \item \textbf{Local constraints} require only the current token. Entity-type and relation-vocabulary membership fall in this class: each candidate token can be checked against the ontology vocabulary independently, which the grammar layer handles via CFG and enum rules.
  \item \textbf{Prefix-decidable constraints} require the current token plus previously generated context. Domain/range constraints are prefix-decidable: once the head entity type and relation type have been generated, the valid tail entity types are fully determined. The semantic layer implements this via a stateful entity registry that tracks decoded types and activates the appropriate logit mask at each type-bearing position.
  \item \textbf{Non-local constraints} require information not yet generated. Forward coreference—where a later mention determines the type of an earlier one—is inherently non-local and falls outside the scope of single-pass left-to-right decoding.
\end{enumerate}
%
OntoCoDec's two-layer design covers the first two classes: grammar for local, semantic for prefix-decidable. The non-local class motivates the two-pass strategy (S2, \S\ref{sec:s2}), which partially addresses cross-field consistency by separating entity extraction from relation generation, though it does not fully resolve forward coreference (\S\ref{sec:limitations}).

% Section 7 — Conclusion
% Data source: Phase 2 SciERC registry experiments + Phase 0 DocRED
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_full_s1,
%          phase0_scierc_unconstrained, phase0_docred_unconstrained
% All numbers verified against registry 2026-05-14.

We presented OntoCoDec, a framework that automatically compiles IE ontology schemas into token-level decoding constraints to enforce type validity at generation time.
Our work makes three contributions.

First, we conducted the first systematic study of ontological constraint violations in LLM-based IE (\S\ref{sec:violation_landscape}).
Across two benchmarks with substantially different ontology sizes---SciERC (7~relations) and DocRED (96~relations)---we found that domain/range violation rates are comparable (15.37\% vs.\ 18.46\%), % exp_ids: phase0_scierc_unconstrained, phase0_docred_unconstrained
indicating that violation severity is driven by \emph{constraint tightness} $\bar{\tau}$ rather than ontology scale.
SciERC ($\bar{\tau}{=}0.333$, mean 24 valid type pairs per relation) and DocRED ($\bar{\tau}{=}0.842$, mean 5.68) exhibit comparable violation rates despite a 14$\times$ difference in ontology size, and within each model, DR reduction scales inversely with $\bar{\tau}$: 94--99\% on SciERC ($\bar{\tau}{=}0.333$) vs.\ 45--90\% on DocRED ($\bar{\tau}{=}0.842$), with the residual modulated by model-specific baseline violation rates (Section~\ref{sec:cross-model}).
% Qwen: SciERC DR↓94%, DocRED DR↓45%; Llama: SciERC DR↓99%, DocRED DR↓90%

Second, we introduced a two-layer constraint architecture that decomposes ontological enforcement into complementary mechanisms:
a \emph{grammar layer} (XGrammar CFG) that eliminates structural violations (RV, ET\,$\to$\,0\%) and a \emph{semantic layer} (TypeConstraintProcessor with a stateful entity registry) that enforces domain/range constraints at the token level. % exp_id: phase2_scierc_grammar_only
The grammar layer serves as an enabling prerequisite for the semantic layer; the two compose via bitwise AND over candidate token sets.

Third, we validated OntoCoDec empirically.
On SciERC, the full system reduces domain/range violations from 15.37\% to 0.93\%---a 94\% relative reduction---while completely eliminating RV and ET violations, with no significant impact on relation F1 ($+$0.13 percentage points, $p > 0.05$). % exp_id: phase2_scierc_full_s1
On DocRED, the full system reduces domain/range violations from 18.46\% to 10.21\%---a 45\% relative reduction---while eliminating RV and ET violations entirely, with statistically significant gains in relation F1 ($+$0.50pp, $p{<}0.001$) and entity F1 ($+$1.23pp, $p{<}0.001$) for Qwen3-8B. Llama-3.1-8B achieves substantial DR reduction (90.2\%, 26.07\%\,$\to$\,2.55\%) with F1-neutral impact. % exp_ids: phase2_docred_full, llama_docred_full_s1, llama_docred_unconstrained
Compared with post-hoc filtering, decoding-time enforcement preserves true positives and eliminates entity-type violations that post-hoc methods cannot address.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
Several limitations qualify these findings.
The semantic layer introduces cross-field consistency (CF) violations: CF rises from 0.08\% under unconstrained decoding to 9.90\% with full constraints. % exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_full_s1
This is a systematic consequence of per-relation independent type enforcement---when the same entity appears across multiple triples, each relation's domain/range constraint may assign it a different type, producing entity-versus-relation type drift.
The grammar layer alone does not elevate CF (0.08\%, matching the unconstrained baseline), confirming that CF is entirely attributable to the semantic layer. % exp_id: phase2_scierc_grammar_only
Resolving this cross-relation type coherence problem is an open challenge, not a trivial implementation fix.
Cross-field consistency violations increase with constraint strength and vary across models: CF reaches 12.02\% for Llama-3.1-8B on DocRED under full constraints, compared with 2.57\% for Qwen3-8B on the same dataset, suggesting that per-relation independent enforcement interacts with model-specific generation patterns. % exp_ids: llama_docred_full_s1, phase2_docred_full
Constrained decoding can increase parse failure rates for some model-dataset combinations: Llama-3.1-8B on DocRED shows 91 parse failures under full constraints versus 68 unconstrained (9.1\% vs.\ 6.8\%), likely due to max-token truncation of longer constrained outputs. All F1 metrics are computed over successfully parsed documents only. % exp_ids: llama_docred_full_s1, llama_docred_unconstrained
Beyond CF, experiments use two models (Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), confirming that constraint enforcement generalizes across model families: Llama-3.1-8B on DocRED achieves a 90.2\% DR reduction (26.07\%\,$\to$\,2.55\%) without any code modification.
% llama_docred_unconstrained: DR=26.07%; llama_docred_full_s1: DR=2.55%
Results are reported for two models and two datasets under zero-shot prompting only, and integration with fine-tuned models has not been explored.

\paragraph{Future Work.}
We identify four directions.
(1)~Extension to larger models (quantized 70B-class) to further verify model-agnostic generalization across scales.
(2)~Global entity-level type consensus during decoding---maintaining a shared entity registry across all relations within an instance---to resolve CF violations.
(3)~Integration with fine-tuned models, combining constraint-aware training objectives with decoding-time enforcement.
(4)~Extension to non-English ontologies to evaluate cross-lingual applicability.

\section{Violation Landscape}
\label{sec:violation_landscape}

Before presenting our constrained decoding framework, we first quantify how frequently LLMs violate ontological constraints during information extraction.
This analysis serves two purposes: it establishes the practical severity of unconstrained generation and identifies which constraint categories demand enforcement at decoding time versus those addressable through prompting alone.

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:violation_setup}

We evaluate a strong open-weight model, Qwen3-8B~\cite{qwen2025qwen3}, under zero-shot greedy decoding on two IE benchmarks that differ substantially in ontological complexity:
\textbf{SciERC}~\cite{luan2018scierc} (551 test sentences, 7 relation types, avg.\ 26.1 valid type pairs per relation) and \textbf{DocRED}~\cite{yao2019docred} (998 dev documents, 96 relation types, avg.\ 5.68 valid type pairs per relation).
Both datasets ship with typed entity and relation schemas, enabling automatic constraint checking.

We measure four categories of ontological violation:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Domain/Range (DR):} a predicted triple $(h,r,t)$ satisfies $(\mathrm{type}(h), \mathrm{type}(t)) \notin \sigma(r)$, where $\sigma(r)$ is the set of valid subject--object type pairs for relation $r$.
    \item \textbf{Relation Vocabulary (RV):} the predicted relation type $r \notin \mathcal{R}$.
    \item \textbf{Entity Type (ET):} the predicted entity type $e \notin \mathcal{E}$.
    \item \textbf{Cross-Field Consistency (CF):} the same entity span is assigned different types across distinct triples within one instance.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Violation Distribution}
\label{sec:violation_distribution}

Table~\ref{tab:prompt_comparison} reports violation rates on both benchmarks.
On SciERC (1{,}724 predicted triples, 2{,}474 entities), domain/range violations affect 15.37\% of triples, while RV, ET, and CF violations are comparatively rare at 1.39\%, 0.40\%, and 0.08\%, respectively.
On DocRED (16{,}540 triples, 19{,}099 entities), DR violations reach 18.70\%---comparable to SciERC despite DocRED's ontology being 14$\times$ larger.
This parity suggests that DR violation rates are driven primarily by \emph{constraint tightness} (valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology size: DocRED averages only 5.68 valid pairs per relation versus SciERC's 26.1.

RV violations on DocRED are dramatically higher (28.90\% vs.\ 1.39\%), indicating that 96 relation types exceed the model's capacity to faithfully reproduce a target vocabulary from a single in-context specification.
ET violations follow a similar trend (7.50\% vs.\ 0.40\%).
CF violations remain negligible on both datasets (0.08\%), suggesting that within-instance type coherence is largely maintained even without explicit enforcement.

\subsection{Per-Relation Analysis}
\label{sec:per_relation}

Figure~\ref{fig:per_relation_dr} breaks down DR violation rates by relation type on SciERC.
Violation rates vary by over 40 percentage points across relations:
\textsc{Compare} exhibits the highest rate at 42.4\% (28/66 triples), followed by \textsc{Feature-of} at 33.5\% (163/486), \textsc{Part-of} at 25.0\% (18/72), and \textsc{Evaluate-for} at 24.1\% (32/133).
At the other extreme, \textsc{Used-for} violates at only 0.76\% (6/787) and \textsc{Conjunction} at 0\% (0/32).

This distribution correlates with constraint tightness: \textsc{Compare} permits only a few valid type pairs in the SciERC schema, leaving minimal room for type substitution, whereas \textsc{Used-for} and \textsc{Conjunction} accept a broad range of subject--object type combinations.
The pattern implies that violations are not random generation noise but systematic failures to satisfy narrow type constraints---precisely the setting where decoding-time enforcement is most needed.

\subsection{Prompt Insufficiency}
\label{sec:prompt_insufficiency}

A natural question is whether explicitly stating domain/range constraints in the prompt suffices to eliminate violations.
We test \emph{schema-informed prompting}, which augments the extraction prompt with the full list of valid type pairs for each relation.

On SciERC, schema-informed prompting reduces DR violations from 15.37\% to 5.78\% (a 62.4\% relative reduction) and lowers RV from 1.39\% to 0.30\% and ET from 0.40\% to 0\% (Table~\ref{tab:prompt_comparison}).
On DocRED, the reduction is weaker: DR drops from 18.70\% to 12.84\% ($-$31.3\%), RV from 28.90\% to 18.40\%, and ET from 7.50\% to 0.61\%.
McNemar's test confirms that all four violation-category improvements are statistically significant ($p < 0.01$) on both datasets.

However, aggregate improvements mask per-relation instability.
On SciERC, schema-informed prompting reduces DR for \textsc{Feature-of} by 22.3 percentage points and \textsc{Part-of} by 22.5~pp, but \emph{increases} DR for \textsc{Evaluate-for} by 5.8~pp (Figure~\ref{fig:per_relation_dr}).
This reversal---where adding constraint information to the prompt worsens compliance on a specific relation---demonstrates that prompt-based approaches lack the guarantee of monotonic improvement across all constraint categories.

Two findings emerge from this analysis.
First, prompt-based schema enforcement scales poorly with ontological complexity: the relative DR reduction on DocRED (31.3\%) is roughly half that on SciERC (62.4\%), and RV violations remain at 18.40\% even after prompting.
Second, even on the simpler SciERC ontology, prompt interventions are unreliable at the per-relation level.
These limitations motivate a decoding-time mechanism that enforces constraints \emph{by construction} rather than by instruction, which we present in Section~\ref{sec:method}.
